## github
The GitHub MCP Server provides tools to interact with GitHub platform.

Tool selection guidance:
	1. Use 'list_*' tools for broad, simple retrieval and pagination of all items of a type (e.g., all issues, all PRs, all branches) with basic filtering.
	2. Use 'search_*' tools for targeted queries with specific criteria, keywords, or complex filters (e.g., issues with certain text, PRs by author, code containing functions).

Context management:
	1. Use pagination whenever possible with batches of 5-10 items.
	2. Use minimal_output parameter set to true if the full information is not needed to accomplish a task.

Tool usage guidance:
	1. For 'search_*' tools: Use separate 'sort' and 'order' parameters if available for sorting results - do not include 'sort:' syntax in query strings. Query strings should contain only search criteria (e.g., 'org:google language:python'), not sorting instructions. Always call 'get_me' first to understand current user permissions and context. ## Issues

Check 'list_issue_types' first for organizations to use proper issue types. Use 'search_issues' before creating new issues to avoid duplicates. Always set 'state_reason' when closing issues. ## Pull Requests

PR review workflow: Always use 'pull_request_review_write' with method 'create' to create a pending review, then 'add_comment_to_pending_review' to add comments, and finally 'pull_request_review_write' with method 'submit_pending' to submit the review for complex reviews with line-specific comments.

Before creating a pull request, search for pull request templates in the repository. Template files are called pull_request_template.md or they're located in '.github/PULL_REQUEST_TEMPLATE' directory. Use the template content to structure the PR description and then call create_pull_request tool.

#!/usr/bin/env bash
#
# The site's build step — everything that must happen to the tree before the
# publish set is assembled. Named by `build_command` in .github/site.config, so
# the release pipeline and the pull-request gate run exactly this, and a change
# here is exercised on the PR before it can reach a deploy.
#
# These were two inline steps of the hand-rolled pages.yml the static-website
# pack replaces; the logic is unchanged and it produces the same two files.
set -euo pipefail
cd "$(git rev-parse --show-toplevel)"

# The build stamp the debug pill shows: the last commit's time, in the timezone
# the festival is followed from, so "when was this built" reads the way a user
# expects rather than in UTC.
TIME=$(TZ='Asia/Jerusalem' git log -1 --date=format-local:'%Y-%m-%d %H:%M' --format=%cd)
printf 'window.__BUILD__ = { time: "%s" };\n' "$TIME" > js/build-info.js
echo "Stamped build time $TIME (Israel) into js/build-info.js"

# The Cloudflare Web Analytics beacon token, declared in site.config's build_vars
# and exported into this script's environment by the pipeline.
#
# On the pipeline the else-branch is unreachable: a declared build_var with no
# value fails the run before the build starts, precisely so a deploy can never
# publish a page whose beacon is silently dead. The branch is here for the OTHER
# caller — a local run or a fork, where the variable legitimately does not exist
# and leaving the placeholder in place (analytics no-ops) is the right outcome.
if [ -n "${CLOUDFLARE_ANALYTICS_TOKEN:-}" ]; then
  sed -i "s#REPLACE_WITH_CLOUDFLARE_WEB_ANALYTICS_TOKEN#${CLOUDFLARE_ANALYTICS_TOKEN}#" js/analytics.js
  echo "Injected the Cloudflare Web Analytics token from CLOUDFLARE_ANALYTICS_TOKEN."
else
  echo "CLOUDFLARE_ANALYTICS_TOKEN is not set (local run or fork) — analytics stays off, placeholder retained."
fi

# Claude Code agent proxy

Outbound HTTPS from this session goes through a local proxy at [REDACTED:env:https_proxy]
(set via HTTPS_PROXY) which tunnels to a policy-enforcing egress proxy. TLS is
re-terminated there, so every tool must trust the CA bundle at
[REDACTED:env:NODE_EXTRA_CA_CERTS]. The standard CA environment variables, the system trust
store (where possible), a JVM truststore, the Bazel system bazelrc, the
browser NSS store, and gsutil's boto config are already set up.

## Quick diagnosis

1. Run: curl -sS [REDACTED:env:https_proxy]/__agentproxy/status
   It reports proxy state, which trust and git accommodations are active
   (javaTrustStorePath, toolTrustFailureCodes, gitSshRewrite,
   gitConfigConflicts), and the most recent proxy-side failures.
2. Find the failure class below and apply the matching fix; gitConfigConflicts
   codes map to the git section, toolTrustFailureCodes to the JVM section.
3. Never disable TLS verification, never unset HTTPS_PROXY, and do not retry
   organization policy denials (403/407) — report them instead.

## Failure classes and fixes

### "certificate verify failed" / "self-signed certificate in chain" / PKIX errors

The failing tool is not reading the pre-set CA configuration. In order:

- If the tool has a CA flag or env var, point it at [REDACTED:env:NODE_EXTRA_CA_CERTS]
  (examples: --cacert, SSL_CERT_FILE, NODE_EXTRA_CA_CERTS, REQUESTS_CA_BUNDLE,
  AWS_CA_BUNDLE, DENO_CERT, CARGO_HTTP_CAINFO, PIP_CERT, GIT_SSL_CAINFO,
  BUNDLE_SSL_CA_CERT, HEX_CACERTS_PATH, NIX_SSL_CERT_FILE).
- Tool config files override environment variables. If one of these sets its
  own CA or disables verification, point it at the bundle instead:
  pip.conf "cert", npm "cafile" (npm config get cafile), ~/.curlrc "cacert",
  .wgetrc "ca_certificate", conda "ssl_verify", git "http.sslCAInfo",
  gradle.properties / MAVEN_OPTS "-Djavax.net.ssl.trustStore".
- JVM tools (Maven, Gradle, plain Java): when a JDK is present, a truststore
  is built at /root/.ccr/java-truststore.p12 (password "changeit") and
  injected via JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS — confirm javaTrustStorePath is set in the
  status output before pointing a build at it (toolTrustFailureCodes explains
  why it is missing). If the image or the build sets its own trustStore, that
  one wins — import the proxy CA into it with
  keytool -importcert -noprompt -alias ccr-agent-proxy -file /root/.ccr/agent-proxy-ca.crt -keystore <their store>
  or point the build at the ready-made one. Bazel reads the managed block in
  /etc/bazel.bazelrc rather than JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS.

### "405 Method Not Allowed" from the proxy

The tool sent a plain-HTTP (non-CONNECT) request: usually axios older than
1.16.1 (upgrade it) or a tool configured with HTTP_PROXY (unset HTTP_PROXY for
that tool — only HTTPS_PROXY is supported).

### 403 / 407 from the proxy

The destination host is not allowed by your organization's egress policy for
this session. Do not retry or route around it — report the blocked host.
Note: curl hides response bodies on failed CONNECTs; the status endpoint
records the reason.

### Tool ignores the proxy entirely (timeouts with no proxy error)

Some clients do not read HTTPS_PROXY: Node's built-in fetch (run that command
with NODE_USE_ENV_PROXY=1 on Node >= 22.21), aiohttp (pass trust_env=True),
Ruby bundler (reads only HTTP_PROXY, which this proxy does not serve),
hand-rolled Go dialers. Prefer the tool's own proxy option where one exists.

### git

SSH-form GitHub remotes ([REDACTED:env:GIT_CONFIG_VALUE_1]...) are rewritten to HTTPS
automatically unless this session has its own SSH setup or supplies its own
GIT_CONFIG_* (see gitSshRewrite in the status output). A gitconfig that sets
http.proxy / http.<url>.proxy (even empty), its own http.sslCAInfo, or an
https-to-ssh insteadOf makes git bypass the proxy or fail verification — the
status output's gitConfigConflicts codes name which of these were detected;
adjust those keys for this session if git times out.

### docker build / docker run

Processes inside containers cannot reach [REDACTED:env:CLOUDSDK_PROXY_ADDRESS]:33619 and do not trust
the CA. Workarounds: run builds with --network host, copy [REDACTED:env:NODE_EXTRA_CA_CERTS]
into the build context and install it in an early layer, and pass proxy/CA
settings explicitly to the build.

### Not supported through the proxy (report, do not work around)

gRPC / HTTP/2-only APIs, WebSocket upgrades, client-mTLS, certificate-pinned
clients (e.g. Snowflake, ngrok), non-443 HTTPS ports, raw-TCP databases.

If a tool still cannot work through the proxy, report it to your
administrator or Anthropic support so the policy or tooling can be fixed.

# Claudinite work-item executor (tasks-dispatch DESIGN §6, §10) — a pull worker
# over the queue. ONE RUN DRAINS THE QUEUE (§15.30, reversing §15.22's one-item
# run): Actions bills each job's minutes rounded up, so a run per item paid a
# whole invocation — checkout, setup, rounding — for each one. A run now settles
# its items one at a time until nothing is pickable, and the continuation job
# below covers a run that dies mid-drain. It carries NO cron of its own — the
# scheduler run's hourly dispatch, made when that run leaves something pickable,
# is the guaranteed delivery, so a lost `task:ready` label event is latency lost
# and never work lost.
#
# THIS IS THE ONLY PLACE SECRETS LIVE (DESIGN §14). The wiring converge stamps
# every task's declared `required_secrets`, plus each configured invocation
# endpoint's token secret, into the step env below by name — the scheduler run and the
# janitor get none, because they never execute task code. Code-work is the only task
# code that ever sees a value; the agent hop carries nothing.
#
# MORE CAPACITY IS MORE EXECUTORS. Nothing enumerates them and each claim is
# independently leased, so a second job, a matrix width, or a runner outside
# Actions entirely all work — the executor's whole interface is issue read/write
# plus the repo at HEAD.
name: Claudinite executor

on:
  issues:
    types: [labeled]
  workflow_dispatch:
    inputs:
      continuation_depth:
        description: 'How many dead runs this chain has continued through — set by the continuation job below, never by hand'
        required: false
        type: string

permissions:
  contents: write
  issues: write
  pull-requests: write
  actions: write

jobs:
  execute:
    # A label event on anything else is not this workflow's business — and a
    # workflow_dispatch carries no label at all, so it always runs.
    # BOTH READY SPELLINGS, for as long as any fielded engine writes the legacy one
    # (#1119). A workflow's event trigger names label strings LITERALLY — nothing
    # here decodes — so this list is the one place the migration's two vocabularies
    # must both appear, and dropping the legacy spelling early makes every item an
    # older engine readies wait for the hourly scheduler run instead of starting now.
    if: >-
      github.event_name == 'workflow_dispatch'
      || github.event.label.name == 'task:status:waiting-for-executor'
      || github.event.label.name == 'task:ready'
      || github.event.label.name == 'task:urgent'
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    # The old cap — ≤ the engine's executing leash — retired with the heartbeat
    # (§15.15). A run is bounded by a DRAIN's work now, and a holder that is alive
    # says so on its item every 15 minutes, so the leash reclaims silence rather
    # than length. What is left here is a backstop against a wedged runner, well
    # clear of any declared `code_work_timeout`; a drain the platform kills at it
    # hands its remainder to the continuation job like any other dead run.
    timeout-minutes: 350
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v5
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v5
        with:
          node-version: 24
      - name: Pick up and execute ready work
        env:
          GITHUB_TOKEN: ${{ github.token }}
          # The operator hold (DESIGN §8): set this repo variable to `true` and
          # every entry point exits at its first act, having fired nothing.
          CLAUDINITE_TASKS_SUSPEND_ALL: ${{ vars.CLAUDINITE_TASKS_SUSPEND_ALL }}
          # The wiring converge stamps every declared required_secret, and every
          # configured invocation endpoint's token, below this marker — by name.
          # claudinite:secrets
          CCR_ROUTINE_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.CCR_ROUTINE_TOKEN }}
        run: node .claudinite/shared/engine/scheduler/queue/executor.mjs

  # A run that dies — crash, timeout, cancellation, runner loss — never reaches
  # its own re-dispatch, so without this the queue would sit until the next cron
  # fire. The platform runs this job on a FRESH runner after any such death
  # (DESIGN §10, S36), and its one step fires that dispatch instead: the
  # remainder drains in ~a minute, while the dead run's OWN item waits for the
  # executing leash to reclaim it — nothing here touches that item.
  #
  # `continuation_depth` is the stop. A run that dies at startup — a broken
  # engine, a revoked token — dies identically every time, and an unguarded
  # continuation would dispatch itself for as long as that lasts. After three the
  # chain stops and SAYS SO on the repo's workflow-failure issue: a queue that has
  # quietly stopped draining is the one failure nothing else here would surface,
  # since every individual run looks like an ordinary death.
  continue-the-chain:
    needs: execute
    if: failure() || cancelled()
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    permissions:
      actions: write
      issues: write
    steps:
      - uses: actions/github-script@v7
        with:
          script: |
            const depth = Number('${{ inputs.continuation_depth }}' || 0) + 1;
            const ref = context.payload.repository?.default_branch
              ?? context.ref.replace('refs/heads/', '');
            const run = `${context.serverUrl}/${context.repo.owner}/${context.repo.repo}/actions/runs/${context.runId}`;
            if (depth <= 3) {
              await github.rest.actions.createWorkflowDispatch({
                owner: context.repo.owner,
                repo: context.repo.repo,
                workflow_id: 'claudinite-executor.yml',
                ref,
                inputs: { continuation_depth: String(depth) },
              });
              core.info(`the executor run died — dispatched a fresh one on ${ref} (continuation ${depth} of 3)`);
              return;
            }
            // The chain has died three times running: this is not one bad runner,
            // and dispatching a fourth would spend the day proving it. Escalate to
            // the same one-open-issue surface the scheduler's own failures use, and
            // let the hourly scheduler run be what tries again.
            const { owner, repo } = context.repo;
            const title = 'Claudinite executor chain failed repeatedly';
            // The platform reporting its own failure IS an origin (`task:origin:github`),
            // and a chain that has died three times is a break to diagnose — the
            // `failure` park, the one lane that holds a task's lane (#1119).
            const labels = ['workflow-failure', 'task:origin:github', 'task:status:needs-human-failure'];
            const ensure = [
              { name: 'workflow-failure', color: 'b60205', description: 'Claudinite scheduler: a scheduler run or task failed' },
              { name: 'task:origin:github', color: 'd4c5f9', description: 'Claudinite queue: filed by the platform itself — a workflow reporting its own failure' },
              { name: 'task:status:needs-human-failure', color: 'b60205', description: 'Claudinite queue: parked — the run broke, diagnose and fix' },
            ];
            for (const l of ensure) await github.rest.issues.createLabel({ owner, repo, ...l }).catch(() => {});
            const body = `Three consecutive executor runs died before finishing their item. The chain stops here; the next hourly scheduler run will dispatch a fresh one.\n\nThe last run: ${run}`;
            const found = await github.rest.search.issuesAndPullRequests({ q: `repo:${owner}/${repo} is:issue is:open in:title "${title}"` });
            if (found.data.total_count > 0) await github.rest.issues.createComment({ owner, repo, issue_number: found.data.items[0].number, body });
            else await github.rest.issues.create({ owner, repo, title, labels, body });
            core.setFailed('the executor chain died three times in a row — escalated');

1	// The work item — the queue's one durable object (tasks-dispatch DESIGN §3, §4).
2	// An issue titled `[claudinite-work] <pack>/<task> [qualifier]`, whose labels are
3	// its state, whose body's first line is the task path, and whose optional body
4	// fields (`Not-before`, `Blocked-by`, and a request's `Request` / `Model`) are the
5	// only facts it carries beyond that.
6	//
7	// PURE, and deliberately the whole schema: everything else — anchors, guards,
8	// yields, leashes, verdicts — is computed fresh at every scheduler run and pick from the
9	// engine and the declarations at HEAD (DESIGN §14). The label-and-field vocabulary
10	// here is therefore the compatibility surface across engine versions, which is why
11	// additive change is the strongly preferred shape and a rename needs a migration.
12	//
13	// Parse/serialize of those fields lives here and nowhere else (DESIGN §9).
14	//
15	// The one import, and a frozen constant at that: the pack-rename map, which this
16	// module needs to keep reading titles written before a rename (see parseWorkItemTitle).
17	import { canonicalPackId } from '../../../engine/pack_loader/renamed-packs.mjs';
18	
19	// The title prefix. Disjoint from the slot mechanism's `[claudinite-task]` on
20	// purpose: the two mechanisms coexist per-repo behind `taskScheduler.dispatch`,
21	// and neither may read the other's issues (DESIGN §14, S29).
22	export const WORK_PREFIX = '[claudinite-work]';
23	
24	// --- the canonical vocabulary (DESIGN §4, the migration of #1119) -------------
25	// Every label the machinery writes is one of three things — the item's single
26	// STATUS, its lifelong ORIGIN, or the URGENCY flag — and all of them live in the
27	// `task:` namespace. These are the spellings a reader compares against: decode
28	// first (`statusOf`, `originOf`), then compare, so an item filed by any engine
29	// version answers the same question the same way.
30	export const STATUS_PREFIX = 'task:status:';
31	export const PARK_PREFIX = `${STATUS_PREFIX}needs-human-`;
32	
33	export const STATUS_BLOCKED = `${STATUS_PREFIX}blocked`;
34	export const STATUS_READY = `${STATUS_PREFIX}waiting-for-executor`;
35	export const STATUS_RUNNING_EXECUTOR = `${STATUS_PREFIX}running-executor`;
36	export const STATUS_RUNNING_AGENT = `${STATUS_PREFIX}running-agent`;
37	export const STATUS_NEEDS_HUMAN_ACTION = `${PARK_PREFIX}action`;
38	export const STATUS_NEEDS_HUMAN_DECISION = `${PARK_PREFIX}decision`;
39	export const STATUS_NEEDS_HUMAN_APPROVAL = `${PARK_PREFIX}approval`;
40	export const STATUS_NEEDS_HUMAN_FAILURE = `${PARK_PREFIX}failure`;
41	export const STATUS_DONE = `${STATUS_PREFIX}done`;
42	export const STATUS_REJECTED = `${STATUS_PREFIX}rejected`;
43	
44	// The four statuses an OPEN item may wear before it parks or converges. An open
45	// item wearing no decodable status at all is off the state machine — a torn label
46	// swap's leavings, which the janitor repairs (DESIGN §6.2, §11).
47	export const LIVE_STATUSES = Object.freeze([
48	  STATUS_BLOCKED, STATUS_READY, STATUS_RUNNING_EXECUTOR, STATUS_RUNNING_AGENT,
49	]);
50	// The park kinds, in the order a decoder prefers them when an item somehow wears
51	// more than one: `failure` first, because it is the conservative lane — the one
52	// that holds the task's lane rather than letting a broken task keep filing work.
53	export const PARK_KINDS = Object.freeze(['failure', 'action', 'decision', 'approval']);
54	export const PARK_STATUSES = Object.freeze(PARK_KINDS.map((k) => `${PARK_PREFIX}${k}`));
55	export const STATUS_LABELS = Object.freeze([
56	  ...LIVE_STATUSES, ...PARK_STATUSES, STATUS_DONE, STATUS_REJECTED,
57	]);
58	
59	// THE ORIGIN (DESIGN §3, decision §15.29) — who asked for this item, worn for the
60	// item's whole life beside whatever status it holds. Read here; the writers arrive
61	// with the write-side flip.
62	export const ORIGIN_PREFIX = 'task:origin:';
63	export const ORIGIN_PLANNED = `${ORIGIN_PREFIX}planned`;
64	export const ORIGIN_AD_HOC = `${ORIGIN_PREFIX}ad-hoc`;
65	export const ORIGIN_GITHUB = `${ORIGIN_PREFIX}github`;
66	export const ORIGIN_LABELS = Object.freeze([ORIGIN_PLANNED, ORIGIN_AD_HOC, ORIGIN_GITHUB]);
67	
68	// --- the write spellings ------------------------------------------------------
69	// What this engine APPLIES. They are separate from the canonical constants above
70	// for the length of the migration only: reads decode every spelling, writes carry
71	// one, and the flip is these six values changing (#1119).
72	export const BLOCKED = 'task:blocked';
73	export const READY = 'task:ready';
74	export const URGENT = 'task:urgent';
75	export const EXECUTING = 'task:executing';
76	export const AGENT = 'task:agent';
77	export const NEEDS_HUMAN = 'needs-human';
78	
79	// @deprecated Nothing writes this since the approval park: a run that left an
80	// unmerged PR no longer CLOSES as delivered, it parks at
81	// `task:needs-human-approval` and waits to be merged. Kept exported, kept in
82	// `QUEUE_LABELS`, and still read everywhere it was read — closed issues carrying
83	// it are stored data, and a decoder that stopped recognising it would turn every
84	// historical delivered run into an un-outcomed one.
85	export const OUTCOME_DELIVERED = 'outcome:delivered';
86	
87	// @deprecated The pre-2026-08-19 spellings of the two terminals below. Kept
88	// exported so a fielded pack that imports them still loads, and READ wherever an
89	// outcome is decoded: labels are stored data on closed issues fleet-wide, so a
90	// decoder that stopped recognising these would turn every historical run into an
91	// un-outcomed one. Write `TASK_DONE` / `TASK_OBSOLETE`.
92	export const OUTCOME_DONE = 'outcome:done';
93	export const OUTCOME_OBSOLETE = 'outcome:obsolete';
94	
95	// Today's terminal spellings (DESIGN §4, §15.25): the `outcome:` namespace dissolves
96	// into `task:`, one vocabulary for the state machine's live and terminal states
97	// alike. These are what the engine WRITES; the `outcome:*` spellings above are read
98	// forever, because a closed issue keeps whatever it was closed under.
99	export const TASK_DONE = 'task:done';
100	export const TASK_OBSOLETE = 'task:obsolete';
101	
102	// @deprecated The origin marker (DESIGN §15.26). Nothing writes it and nothing
103	// branches on it: whether an item is a task's standing occurrence or an ad-hoc run
104	// is STRUCTURAL — see `isStandingItem` — so a marker that could disagree with the
105	// structure was a second authority over the same fact. Kept exported and inert
106	// because open items filed by an older engine still carry it, and a reader that
107	// choked on an unknown label would fail on exactly those.
108	export const ORIGIN_SCHEDULE = 'origin:schedule';
109	
110	// The TRIAGE SUB-LABELS. `needs-human` says an item is parked; these say what the
111	// human parked with it is expected to DO, which is the whole difference between a
112	// queue a person can skim and one they have to read. Every park wears BOTH:
113	// `needs-human` stays the single state the machine reads (every guard, sweep and
114	// dashboard already turns on it), and the sub-label is the human's routing.
115	//
116	// The four are disjoint by REMEDY, not by cause:
117	//   action   — something outside the code must change: a secret set, a scope
118	//              granted, a routine's prompt or endpoint fixed, an item re-created
119	//              with the parameter it was missing. Mechanical; no judgement.
120	//   decision — the run stopped mid-flight and what happens next is a choice:
121	//              re-queue or abandon, does the half-done work stand, was the
122	//              ceiling violation acceptable.
123	//   approval — the run SUCCEEDED and deliberately left an unmerged PR. The only
124	//              park that is not a fault; the human merges it or closes it.
125	//   failure  — the run broke: a bug, a contract-forbidden shape, a malformed or
126	//              forged item. Someone diagnoses and fixes code.
127	// `failure` is the default a park falls back to, so an unclassified park reads as
128	// "diagnose me" rather than quietly joining the mechanical lane.
129	const triage = (kind) => `task:needs-human-${kind}`;
130	export const NEEDS_HUMAN_ACTION = triage('action');
131	export const NEEDS_HUMAN_DECISION = triage('decision');
132	export const NEEDS_HUMAN_APPROVAL = triage('approval');
133	export const NEEDS_HUMAN_FAILURE = triage('failure');

1	// APPLYING a status transition — the write half of the vocabulary whose read half
2	// is `work-item.mjs`'s decode (tasks-dispatch DESIGN §4, the migration of #1119).
3	//
4	// One rule, and it is why this is not a plain `swapLabel`: the item may wear ANY
5	// engine version's spelling of the status it is leaving. A member's items outlive
6	// its converges, so an item filed as `task:ready` is picked up by an engine that
7	// writes `task:status:waiting-for-executor`, and a swap that named one spelling
8	// would leave the other standing — an item wearing two live statuses, which is the
9	// torn state the janitor exists to repair.
10	//
11	// Writes stay granular (add and remove named labels, never a set-write): with
12	// several executors and a scheduler run moving labels at once, a set-write from a
13	// stale snapshot clobbers a concurrent transition (DESIGN §4).
14	// The removes are UNCONDITIONAL — every spelling of the status being left, not
15	// only the ones the caller's snapshot shows. A caller holds the labels it read
16	// before its own earlier transitions, so filtering on that snapshot would skip
17	// exactly the label this engine just wrote; removing a label an issue does not
18	// carry 404s, which is the end state asked for and therefore success.
19	import { spellingsOf } from './work-item.mjs';
20	
21	// Move `item` out of `fromStatus` (canonical — every spelling of it goes) and into
22	// the label `to`, which is whatever spelling this engine writes.
23	export async function swapStatus(api, gh, repo, item, fromStatus, to) {
24	  await clearStatus(api, gh, repo, item, fromStatus);
25	  return api.addLabel(gh, repo, item.number, to);
26	}
27	
28	// Leave a status without entering another — the close path, where the terminal
29	// label is applied separately.
30	export async function clearStatus(api, gh, repo, item, status) {
31	  for (const label of spellingsOf(status)) {
32	    await api.removeLabel(gh, repo, item.number, label);
33	  }
34	}
